newsitem.title: USA: Fed looks beyond benign US inflation environment.
newsitem.headline: Fed looks beyond benign US inflation environment.

text.p: The Federal Reserve signalled its commitment to battling inflation before it manifests itself at the consumer price level by hiking interest rates for the first time in over two years on Tuesday.

The move had been widely anticipated by members of the Wall Street investment community, but in the eyes of some experts, who lauded the current benign price environment, its justification was questionable.

The most recent inflation data available showed that producer prices actually fell by 0.4 percent in February, their biggest decline in over two years, while consumer prices edged higher at a palatable 0.3 percent pace.

Wages -- although rising in real terms -- are hardly soaring, and to many, all of these price indicators are less of a concern than they were in August of last year when the Fed decided to hold rates steady.

"Greenspan is tightening on his expectations that as the economy continues this strong it's going to sometime down the road cause inflation," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.

"I think he can get away with one tightening without any inflation evidence to point to, but by the time it comes around to a second or third tightening he will need something more concrete than a forecast."
The Fed characterized its quarter-percentage-point increase in the federal funds rate as a "prudent step" to extend the economic expansion, which is in its seventh year.
What worries the Fed, and many economists on Wall Street, is that U.S. economic growth is running well above a level which is sustainable.
Gross domesic product registered brisk 3.9 percent growth in the fourth quarter of 1996 and is expected to come in near 3.0 percent in the first quarter.
With wages on the rise and an economy at near-full capacity, the fear is that it is only a matter of time before companies begin passing on higher costs and consumer prices pick up.
"What is being pre-empted here really is the pass through from wages to prices," said Ed McKelvey, senior economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co.
"The economy is growing at a rate which appears to be in excess of its sustainable rate with potential downward pressure on the unemployment rate at a time when it's already quite low."
But some economists see little reason for preemptive action given an environment of intensified global competition which has forced companies to increase productivity without raising prices.

Former Fed Vice Chairman Alan Blinder told Reuters last week that he would not vote for a tightening if he were still at the Fed because the "experiment" the central bank has been running to let growth rise and unemployment slip has so far not resulted in higher inflation.
Larry Chimerine, managing director at the Economic Strategy Institute, a Washington think tank, would also have preferred to see the Fed wait for concrete signs of inflation before acting.
"More often than not we've seen price cutting, price wars and discounting rather than price increases," he said.
"I think a hike is not justified in the slightest," he added. "There is no inflation and there are no signs of inflation."
But even those Wall Street experts who were skeptical of the need for higher rates said a 25 basis point rise was of limited risk to the economy.

In the aftermath of Tuesday's rate hike, many Fed watchers were forecasting a series of further tightenings in the months to come. But should the March 25 hike ultimately prove excessively preemptive, they refused to rule out corrective action from the Fed later in the year.

"Greenspan believes it's less costly to unwind a premature tightening than it is to fall behind the inflation curve," said CIBC's Liro. "If the economy and particularly the consumer started to come off the boil precipitously the Fed could reverse course down the road."
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
